---
title: "The City on My Homepage Was Never a Plan"
description: "There was one building, and suddenly a lot of undoing."
date: YYYY-MM-DD
categories: [infographic]
draft: true
---

If you've landed on my homepage, you've met the city.
It's an illustrated skyline where each building is a different part of what I do, research, teaching, the blog, and clicking one takes you somewhere real. People ask me about it fairly often, including complete strangers, and the honest answer to "how did you plan this" is that I didn't. There was no blueprint, no master sketch of a skyline waiting to be filled in. There was one building.

I never kept a journal of how this thing came together, which is a slightly embarrassing admission so I will take no more questions. If I don't log something somewhere, be it Logseq, a paper notebook, or apparently now a git repository, I lose the order events happened in almost immediately. So before writing this, I went back through the commit history of this website's repository instead of trying to reconstruct a tidier story from memory, which would have been the easier and less honest option. Commit messages from over a year ago are not written for an audience. They're written by someone in a hurry, moving on to the next thing, and reading them back now feels a bit like going through a stranger's shorthand. What follows is what the log actually shows, corrected in a couple of places by what I actually remember, because it turns out the two don't fully agree.

## One building, twice redone

The first icon I ever made for this project was the research building. It's modeled on the real building at the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behaviour, where I worked for more than six years, first as a PhD student and later as a postdoc. At the time I drew it, there was no city and no plan for one. There was just one icon, of one real place, made because I wanted a small picture of the building that had taken up most of my adult life so far.

It's also the only icon in the whole city modeled on somewhere real, which is probably why it took the longest. I redid it twice before it looked right, both times because of mistakes with the isometric lines in Inkscape: get one angle slightly wrong and a building stops reading as the building you were picturing, it just becomes a shape. A research icon that doesn't remind me of the actual place defeats the point of drawing it from a real building at all.

None of that shows up cleanly in the log. Git only preserves what gets committed, and I clearly iterated on this one locally more than I ever committed, because the file history shows exactly one substantial rewrite of research.svg, nine days after it first appeared. Whatever the first two attempts looked like, they never made it into a commit of their own. They just stopped existing.

## The jump to a city

Here's the part I got wrong when I first sat down to write this, and only caught because I checked. I remembered the city growing one building at a time, over some stretch of weeks, the way these things feel like they must have happened. The commit history says otherwise. The research icon sits alone in the repository for nine days. Then, in a single commit, six icons and the entire city background arrive at once: contact, home, illustrations, open science, talks and workshops, and the full skyline underneath them.

So there wasn't a slow accretion, one drawing quietly getting company over months. There was research, alone, for a little over a week, and then a decision, and then most of a city arriving in one sitting. I'd like to say I remember making that decision, but I don't, not really. What I do half-remember is the Max Planck Society's own website having something similar: an illustrated city where different buildings pointed at different institutes and programmes. I've since lost the link, obviously, which feels appropriate for a post about how bad I am at keeping track of where things came from.

Even that first big commit carries a small, honest fingerprint of how quickly it was assembled: sitting alongside the finished icons is a stray duplicate of the entire city background, saved under its own filename inside the icons folder, where it had no reason to be. Nobody cleaned that up before committing it. It's still there in the history.

## What the log actually shows

The rest of the git history isn't a tidy record of steady progress either. It's a record of things being redrawn, resized, and occasionally broken, because they didn't work the first time.

The clearest example is the canvas itself. The little R script that positions every icon on the page reads the canvas dimensions straight out of Inkscape, and those numbers changed three separate times as the artwork grew: starting at roughly 4715 by 2824 pixels, then 5754 by 3235, then 5989 by 3508, and finally 5989 by 3718, where it sits today. Every time that canvas size changed, every single icon's recorded position had to be recalculated, because a position that's correct against one canvas size is wrong against another.

One of those resizes came bundled with some cleanup: a commit from September 2025 that updated the canvas also quietly deleted a Google Scholar scraping script that had been sitting inside the same file for months, and fixed a run of typos scattered through the icon coordinates where commas had crept in where periods should be. Inkscape reads those numbers out with a comma. R wants a dot. Every single coordinate gets copied and pasted across that gap, and every single time there's a small bet running in the background over which decimal convention wins. Small thing. Also the kind of thing that would have made the whole script fail if I'd tried to run it.

There's also a commit from October 2025 called, without further explanation, "fixed city image." I went in expecting a rewrite and found fifteen lines changed in each direction, a genuinely small fix. The big rewrite happened two days later, in a commit that added a pier to the skyline and redrew the talks and workshops icon at the same time, a change large enough that it touched close to four and a half thousand lines across both files. I can't tell you from the commit message alone what was wrong with the pier or the icon before that, only that whatever existed wasn't good enough to keep, and got rebuilt rather than patched. Two days is not a long gestation period for a decision like that.

What I didn't expect to find was how early the personality of the city showed up. The same commit that substantially rewrote the research icon, nine days after the beginning, also added a whole sheet of decorative extras: benches, streetlamps, a bus stop, a bed of sunflowers, a campfire, a tent. All the small props that make the city read as a place instead of ten labeled boxes on a background arrived almost immediately, not as something bolted on once the important buildings existed.

Reading through all of this in one sitting was a strange experience, because it's the closest thing I have to a diary of a project I never actually kept a diary of. Instead of dated entries about how I felt, I have terse commit messages and diff sizes, and I have to reconstruct the feeling from the size of the rewrite. A two-line tweak is confidence. A rewrite of thousands of lines two days after the last one is someone who looked at what they'd just shipped and didn't like it.

None of this reads like a plan being executed. It reads like a thing getting redrawn until it stopped being wrong, by someone who apparently cannot be trusted to remember the order any of it happened in without a log to check.

## How the icons actually line up

The two questions people ask most, once they're done asking whether the city is a single drawing (it is, one Inkscape file, everything else layers on top of it), are some version of: how do the icons sit on the background so precisely, and did you do that by hand.

The mechanism is simpler than it looks. Each icon needs three numbers to sit correctly: its horizontal position, its vertical position, and its width, all read directly off the artwork in Inkscape. Once resized to 100% so the width reading is accurate, those numbers get logged for every icon, alongside the total width and height of the canvas itself.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# canvas size from Inkscape - find it in "Document Properties"
canvas_width <- 5989.414
canvas_height <- 3718.340

# icons positions and sizes
# X and Y are in the move tab in "Transform"
# Width is in the scale tab, but resize to 100% before checking the width in px
icons <- list(
  contact = list(x = 2254.204, y = 679.325, w = 983.975),
  research = list(x = 1561.630, y = 732.550, w = 1240.664)
  # ...one entry per building
)
```
:::


From there, the script converts each icon's raw pixel position into a percentage of the canvas, and those percentages become plain CSS: `top`, `left`, and `width` for each icon, layered as absolutely positioned elements over the background image.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
calc_css <- function(x, y, w) {
  list(
    top   = round((y / canvas_height) * 100, 2),
    left  = round((x / canvas_width) * 100, 2),
    width = round((w / canvas_width) * 100, 2)
  )
}
```
:::


Working in percentages rather than raw pixels is the entire trick. However large or small the city ends up being rendered on someone's screen, phone or desktop, the icons scale together with the background instead of drifting apart from it, because every position is relative to the same canvas rather than fixed to an absolute pixel count. It's not hand-tuned per icon by eye. It's read once out of Inkscape and converted, which is also exactly why the canvas resizing twice was such a headache: it meant redoing that reading for every single building on the map, not just the new ones.

So the answer to "is it precise because you're careful with a mouse" is no, it's precise because a mouse was never involved in the final placement at all. The care went into building a system that turns an Inkscape reading into a percentage once, correctly, so that I never again have to eyeball whether an icon is sitting in the right spot on a browser window of some size I didn't test.

## Still not done

The city gets new versions. Buildings get added, old icons get redrawn, the pier that showed up in October wasn't there a year earlier and won't be the last addition either. There's no final version of this thing sitting somewhere waiting to be reached.

I know this because while writing this post, I found a bug that's currently live in the script. The coffee kiosk icon's position reads `y = 2129,387` instead of `y = 2129.387`, sitting in the file right now. Comma, not dot. I lost that bet again, same as I lost it in every commit before the September 2025 cleanup, which was supposed to have gotten rid of it for good. If I tried to run the script today, it would fail before it got anywhere near the CSS.

It started as a picture of one building I used to work in, before I had any idea it would need neighbors, or that the neighbors would show up in one afternoon instead of the slow unfolding I was so sure I remembered.
